newsitem.title: UK: Superlatives galore as pundits assess UK election.
newsitem.headline: Superlatives galore as pundits assess UK election.

text.p: Political pundits spun superlatives and reached for the history books on Friday in attempts to measure the monumental scale of Labour's British election victory.
The size of the switch in the parties' shares of the vote across the country clearly astonished the experts.

"It is the first election where over 100 seats have changed hands. I have to stress the scale of the change because on the whole the swing was quite uniform," said David Butler of Oxford University, who has analysed trends in voting patterns in every post-1945 parliamentary election and is reputed to have coined the name of the science, psephology.
The largest Labour majority forecast by Reuters panel of 20 experts in voting behaviour this week was for 153 seats.
The BBC forecast the final results would show a Labour majority of 181 seats on an average swing of 10.4 percent.

Opinion polls on the eve of the election pointed to a Labour majority of more than 200 seats. But all commentators were cautious about extrapolating poll findings into seats after a disastrous experience before the 1992 election, when all the polls wrongly forecast Labour would win.

"This is an extraordinary result...There's been nothing like it in this century" said Essex University professor of government Anthony King after television exit polls on Thursday night signalled a huge majority for the opposition party.

As the night unfolded and the BBC's "Swingometer" graphics showed hundreds of constituencies in the 659-seat new parliament switching Labour red from Conservative blue, political scientists raced to call the moment historic.
"The most dramatic election since 1945," Plymouth University politics professor Colin Rallings told ITN television.
"We'll not be certain about how far the Conservatives have fallen until later...but this could be the lowest share of the vote they've got in any election since 1834. That's a staggering thought."
By 0745 GMT, with results still coming in, Labour had won 417 seats and the Conservatives 160. The Liberal Democrats had taken 41 seats and other parties 11.

Another politics professor, Michael Thrasher, commenting for Sky News, took the exit polls as a sign the election was of "historic proportions" but unlike Rallings, his fellow researcher at Plymouth, thought 1832 was the previous record for such a low Conservative result.
History of a more recent kind was made for polling guru Bob Worcester, chairman of the MORI research organisation, in Labour's resounding recapture of the seat in Basildon, Essex, east England.
"A key result in the 1992 election was the winning of 'Essex man' in Basildon," Worcester told CNN Television as Basildon swung 15 percent to Labour.

"That was a triumph of the Conservative party because it meant that John Major, against the polls, was winning that election. But Essex man is dead." 'Essex man' typified a skilled worker won over to the Conservatives by Margaret Thatcher's policies of mass privatisation and home ownership.

"People didn't quite believe the swing would ever happen like this. Despite the fact that all through the campaign we were seeing opinion polls predicting precisely this kind of swing," Rallings said.
As Labour supporters celebrated across the country and Conservatives smarted from the unseating of cabinet ministers, the pundits pored over maps to see what had happened.

The Conservatives stood to lose all representation in Scotland and Wales. Experts said the ousting of a single "unionist" party in these regions represented a fundamental constitutional change and a bodyblow to the Conservative party in its present form.

"The Conservatives have a real problem in reconstructing themselves as a national party. They are hardly there in urban Britain, and not there in Scotland or Wales. They're now completely a party of the suburbs and shires of England," independent analyst Peter Kellner told the BBC.

"They've been wiped out...they've lost cities they used to control. Their membership is falling. All the things that create a functioning party at local level...have ceased to exist in large parts of Britain."
Ivor Crewe, vice-chancellor at Essex University, warned of troubles ahead for both parties.

"(Blair) is going to meet trouble because he will find government a lot harder than he imagines. He will be looking over his shoulder, and it won't be at the old left. The divisions will be different, possibly on Europe, possibly on constitutional issues."

"The Conservative party will find it very difficult to oppose a Labour government that has got such a whopping majority in the House of Commons. They are going to be deeply divided now as to what lesson is to be learned from this election -- were they not euro-sceptical enough, did they not concentrate especially on the economy?" Crewe said.
